title: 10 Jev project ideas with practical starting points
description: Ten Jev project ideas with verified starting points: inbox triage, RAG filtering, model routing, SQL classification and PR review, plus costs and limits.

source.title: Top 10 Jev Builds You Can Ship in an Afternoon

guide_authors.name: Appit Studio
guide_authors.role: Editorial guide; AI-assisted drafting and technical review

connections.step: Build 1: route email into a reviewable action queue
connections.why: The Python app asks seven typed questions per thread and applies queue rules in code. It illustrates the article's inbox pattern, but does not implement Hassan's fraud cascade.
connections.limitations: MIT source-build app; Python 3.10+, uv and a TypeSafe key; optional Gmail IMAP credentials. Live mail text goes to TypeSafe and incurs provider charges. Source reviewed, no live inbox or model test.

connections.step: Build 3: filter retrieved passages before answer generation
connections.why: The Python library's relevance_rerank filters candidate passages by a score threshold, matching the article's delete rather than reorder idea.
connections.limitations: MIT Python 3.11+ package, separate TypeSafe key and usage charges. Query and passages go to TypeSafe. It cannot fix missed retrieval; errors must be handled by the caller. No live calls here.

connections.step: Build 5: prune stale agent tool call and result pairs
connections.why: The MIT TypeScript library implements keep, truncate and drop decisions for paired tool records; the article names Tamara Tran's idea but not this repository.
connections.limitations: Live use needs TypeSafe access and sends transcript excerpts. Jev does not see result bodies and the library does not summarize prose; cache rewrites and repeated work need separate evaluation. Optional host hook not tested here.

connections.step: Build 6: choose a model for a coding-agent turn
connections.why: Rody names jev-router. Its local proxy sends prompt and model candidates to TypeSafe and applies code-owned fallback policy before forwarding a turn to Claude Code or Codex.
connections.limitations: MIT Node.js proxy; requires authenticated coding CLI and a TypeSafe key, with separate provider costs. Prompt and routing metadata leave the machine. CLI compatibility and savings were not tested here.

connections.step: Build 7: classify selected PostgreSQL rows by semantic predicate
connections.why: The extension's jev and jev_prob SQL functions show how to apply TypeSafe decisions to selected rows, related to the Zachi example the article describes.
connections.limitations: PostgreSQL License; PostgreSQL 14–17, PL/Python, server installation privilege, HTTPS and a TypeSafe key required. Live selected row data leaves the server; read-ahead can submit more rows than the final LIMIT. No live SQL run here.

connections.step: Build 10: label pull requests for human review
connections.why: This separate MIT app and GitHub Action asks typed PR questions and applies a code-owned policy. It is not DiffJury or the unnamed Action in the article.
connections.limitations: MIT TypeScript app/Action; requires TypeSafe key and sends PR title, body and selected diff evidence. It can post a comment and fail CI when configured. Source reviewed; no live model or Action test here.

faqs.question: What is the easiest Jev project to build first?
faqs.answer: Start with a synthetic inbox triage queue. A fixed team menu, a deadline question and a review fallback let you inspect every answer before connecting private mail or taking an action.

faqs.question: Can every Jev project here be shipped in an afternoon?
faqs.answer: No. The article's time claim is a prompt to prototype, not a verified delivery estimate. Database extensions, agent hooks, inbox permissions and review workflows may require substantially more setup and evaluation.

faqs.question: Does a high confidence score make an automatic action safe?
faqs.answer: No. Confidence measures how concentrated a Choice or Score answer is, not whether the answer is correct. Test the decision against labeled cases, keep deterministic rules in code and route uncertain or consequential cases to review.

faqs.question: How much will these projects cost to run?
faqs.answer: Cost depends on input tokens, request volume, retries and any fallback model or human review. TypeSafe listed Jev 1.13 at $0.042 per million input tokens on 26 September 2026, with free output tokens; the article's project figures are their builders' reports, not your forecast.
